answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Azure Cosmos DB (the service historically called DocumentDB) uses the resource provider namespace Microsoft.DocumentDB and the main account resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (core CLI). Example create command: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRG --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2 --default-consistency-level Session

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (top-level); MongoDB database and collection nested resource types are Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases and Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases/collections. Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account (set kind = "MongoDB" and appropriate capabilities), plus azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database and azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection for DBs and collections.

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical MongoDB API connection string for a Cosmos account: either SRV form or standard. Example (standard TLS port): mongodb://<username>:<password>@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000&appName=@myaccount@. SRV form: mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false. Host suffix: .mongo.cosmos.azure.com; port (non-SRV) 10255; required options include ssl=true (TLS), replicaSet=globaldb and typically retryWrites=false for Cosmos Mongo compatibility.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Cosmos (DocumentDB/Mongo API) is billed primarily with throughput (Request Units per second) for provisioned throughput accounts (including autoscale/auto-provisioning). There is also a serverless option for supported accounts and autoscale RU options. Recent offerings add vCore-based options for certain SKUs, but the canonical model for Mongo API samples is RU/s provisioned or serverless consumption.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Data-plane access for the MongoDB API is via MongoDB credentials (SCRAM username/password stored in the Cosmos account). Management operations use Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) via ARM roles. As of my knowledge cutoff, Entra ID based data-plane authentication (AAD token directly in the MongoDB driver) is not generally supported for the MongoDB API — drivers authenticate with the Mongo/SCRAM credentials; Azure AD is used for management/ARM operations. Use standard MongoDB auth (username/password / SCRAM) in the driver.

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: For the data plane use the official MongoDB drivers (Node.js mongodb, pymongo, Java MongoDB driver, etc.) since Cosmos DB exposes the MongoDB wire protocol. There is no separate proprietary data-plane SDK for Mongo API; use azure-cosmos SDK only for Cosmos SQL API/other management scenarios and the az SDK for management operations.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: If the cluster has vector capabilities enabled, index types exposed in samples include HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. The Mongo-style command to create a vector index is a createIndex call on the collection with a vector index spec; e.g. db.products.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { method: 'HNSW', dimensions: 1536, metric: 'cosine' }). (Note: exact option names vary by provider/version; treat this as the concrete form to try against the cluster.)

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text and hybrid (text + vector) search for Cosmos DB data is typically accomplished by integrating with Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) or by using the service's built-in search features if the account offers integrated vector+text search. In practice you index documents into Azure Cognitive Search for rich textual ranking and combine that with vector search results for hybrid queries.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Cosmos Mongo API exposes a MongoDB wire protocol version mapped to specific server versions; historically supported versions have included 3.6, 4.0, 4.2, 4.4 and later added 5.x/6.x in previews. Newer accounts may support 6.0/7.0 wire protocol in preview. Not all MongoDB server features are supported: server-side JavaScript, some aggregation stages or newer commands, multi-document transactions across partitions (transactions are limited to items in a single logical partition), and some admin commands may be unsupported or behave differently. Always check the account's configured MongoDB API version for exact feature availability.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is an Azure Cosmos DB Emulator (Windows and a Linux container image) but historically it primarily supports the SQL/Core API; MongoDB API compatibility in the emulator has been limited. For realistic MongoDB-protocol testing use a real Cosmos account or run a local MongoDB server (docker image mongo:latest) on port 27017 for driver-level development — but note behavior differs from Cosmos. If you must use an emulator, use the official Azure Cosmos DB Emulator (example container image mcr.microsoft.com/cosmosdb/linux/azure-cosmos-emulator) and confirm Mongo API support for your emulator version.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change stream support depends on the MongoDB API compatibility level of the Cosmos account. In many supported versions Cosmos offers change stream-like functionality but historically change streams were not fully supported or were limited; some accounts/versions now support change streams. No special portal toggle is usually required beyond having the appropriate MongoDB server compatibility version enabled on the account. (Check the account's MongoDB feature/version for exact support.)

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the service-specific 'documentdb' MCP server profile (the skill_md refers to a documentdb MCP profile named default) for data-plane inspection tools. The general Azure MCP server covers management plane (ARM) operations, but for collection-level data-plane inspection the documentdb MCP server/profile is the one to use.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Microsoft originally marketed the service as Azure DocumentDB. It was rebranded/expanded into Azure Cosmos DB (a multi-model globally distributed database). The Cosmos DB service exposes multiple APIs including SQL (Core), MongoDB-compatible API, Cassandra, Gremlin and Table. The name DocumentDB in other contexts (open-source projects or AWS DocumentDB) is unrelated; Azure DocumentDB was the precursor name for Cosmos DB's document model.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: The underlying engine is Cosmos DB's proprietary distributed storage/compute engine that translates or implements the MongoDB wire protocol. In practice you use standard MongoDB drivers and application code is largely unchanged, but server behavior/limits differ (partitioning, RU model, some unsupported commands, transactional limits and subtle differences in query/aggregation semantics). Expect to test queries and indexes against the Cosmos account rather than assuming identical behavior to a stock MongoDB server.

answers.question: Where should the sample read the Azure DocumentDB connection string from at runtime?
answers.answer: Read the connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime. If DOCUMENTDB_URI is missing or empty the app should exit with a clear error message telling the user to set DOCUMENTDB_URI (or populate a config file) instead of continuing.

answers.question: What database name and collections will this sample use?
answers.answer: Use the database named sample_retail_02 for all sample data. Create collections named transactions (holds purchase transactions) and products (product metadata).

answers.question: Which Node.js client and connection invocation will the sample use?
answers.answer: Use the official Node.js MongoDB driver (npm package mongodb). Connect with MongoClient: const client = new MongoClient(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { tls: true, useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true }); await client.connect(); Then use client.db('sample_retail_02').collection('transactions') etc.

answers.question: What vector index definition will the sample create for nearest-neighbour search?
answers.answer: Create a vector index on the embedding field with a method and dimensions; for example: db.transactions.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { method: 'HNSW', dimensions: 1536, metric: 'cosine' }). (If the cluster supports DiskANN or IVF, swap method accordingly. Use this form as the index create command to run against the cluster.)

answers.question: How should the ingestion script load 20,000 purchase transactions efficiently?
answers.answer: Use bulk inserts in batches (e.g., batches of 500–1000 documents). In Node.js use collection.insertMany(batch, { ordered: false }) or bulkWrite with unordered operations. Include fields: { transactionId, userId, items: [ productId, qty ], timestamp, embedding: [float...] } and commit batches sequentially to avoid request size/timeouts.
